issues.body:
## Description
Generalize the paged-attention execution config introduced in #6099 from `TpuPagedAttentionConfig` to a backend-neutral `PagedAttentionConfig` draccus choice family.

The current config combines backend selection with TPU-specific tuning fields. That is already awkward for `tpu-inference` versus JAX RPA, and it will get worse once a GPU implementation lands. Keep the policy passed through decode, but make the config type generic and dispatch by concrete choice type rather than a TPU-only enum.

Suggested choices: `auto`, `reference`, `tpu-inference`, `jax-rpa`, and later a GPU backend choice.

### Definition of Done
- `decode` and attention call sites accept `PagedAttentionConfig`, not `TpuPagedAttentionConfig`.
- TPU-specific tunables live only on TPU-specific choice dataclasses.
- `paged_attention_with_kv_update` dispatches by config choice type.
- Existing TPU paged-attention tests cover the renamed/generic config surface.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue and AGENTS / fix-issue / author-pr skills
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (PR #6099, related issues)
- [x] Inspect `TpuPagedAttentionConfig`, dispatch, and call sites on the #6099 branch
- [x] Decide on PR vs analysis: posting analysis (depends on #6099; design change spans 5+ files)

**Research**

The code this issue refers to lives only on the open draft [PR #6099](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6099) (`codex/levanter-tpu-paged-attention`); nothing matching `TpuPagedAttentionConfig` / `paged_attention_with_kv_update` is on `main` yet. The current `TpuPagedAttentionConfig` mixes three concerns: backend selection (generic), dispatch policy (`allow_autotune`, `fail_on_reference_fallback` — generic), and backend-specific tunables (`tpu_inference_out_dtype`, `preserve_attention_output_dtype` for tpu-inference; `num_kv_pages_per_block`, `num_queries_per_block`, `vmem_limit_bytes` for JAX RPA). Dispatch is a string-enum if/elif chain in `_run_backend`, so adding a GPU backend later means widening every model signature and growing the enum/branch list.

Relevant code (PR #6099 branch):
- [`tpu_kernels.py#L22-L41`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/levanter-tpu-paged-attention/lib/levanter/src/levanter/inference/tpu_kernels.py#L22-L41) — `TpuPagedAttentionBackend` enum + `TpuPagedAttentionConfig` dataclass.
- [`tpu_kernels.py#L301-L396`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/levanter-tpu-paged-attention/lib/levanter/src/levanter/inference/tpu_kernels.py#L301-L396) — `_run_backend` / `paged_attention_with_kv_update` enum dispatch and fallback chain.
- [`attention.py#L1777`, `#L1961`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/levanter-tpu-paged-attention/lib/levanter/src/levanter/layers/attention.py#L1777) — call sites in `PagedKvCacheAttention.decode` variants.
- [`llama.py#L357`, `#L431`, `#L641`, `#L685`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/levanter-tpu-paged-attention/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/llama.py#L357) and [`apertus.py#L301`, `#L363`, `#L484`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/levanter-tpu-paged-attention/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/apertus.py#L301) — model decode signatures.
- [`test_tpu_paged_attention_backends.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/levanter-tpu-paged-attention/lib/levanter/tests/inference/test_tpu_paged_attention_backends.py), [`test_qwen3.py#L18`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/levanter-tpu-paged-attention/lib/levanter/tests/test_qwen3.py#L18) — tests that construct the config.

**Proposed Approach (for review before implementing)**

Treat this as a design change to land **after** #6099 merges; opening a parallel PR off the draft branch would conflict. Suggested shape:

1. New module `lib/levanter/src/levanter/inference/paged_attention_config.py`:
   - Abstract base `PagedAttentionConfig` registered with draccus as a choice family.
   - Generic policy fields on the base: `fail_on_reference_fallback: bool`, plus multi-backend ordering handled via a wrapper like `AutoPagedAttentionConfig(candidates=...)` rather than a magic `AUTO` enum value.
   - Concrete choices: `ReferencePagedAttentionConfig`, `JaxRpaPagedAttentionConfig` (holds `num_kv_pages_per_block`, `num_queries_per_block`, `vmem_limit_bytes`), `TpuInferencePagedAttentionConfig` (holds `out_dtype`, `preserve_attention_output_dtype`, `vmem_limit_bytes`), and later `GpuPagedAttentionConfig`.
   - Each choice exposes a `run(q, new_k, new_v, kv_cache, batch_info, *, sm_scale, soft_cap) -> tuple[NamedArray, KvPageCache]` method; `paged_attention_with_kv_update` becomes a thin entry point that walks the candidate list, catches `UnsupportedPagedAttentionBackend`, and emits a fallback warning. No `if/elif backend == ...` chain remains.

2. Rename the `tpu_paged_attention` parameter on `PagedKvCacheAttention.decode`, `LlamaDecoderLayer.decode`, `LlamaTransformer.decode`, `LlamaLMHeadModel.decode`, and the Apertus equivalents to `paged_attention: PagedAttentionConfig`. Default to `AutoPagedAttentionConfig()`.

3. Keep `TpuPagedAttentionShape` and platform/shape gating helpers, but move them into the TPU-specific choice classes (they call `tpu_paged_attention_supports_shape` internally). No backward-compat shim per AGENTS.md "NO BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY".

4. Update `test_tpu_paged_attention_backends.py` and `test_qwen3.py` to construct concrete choices (`JaxRpaPagedAttentionConfig()`, `TpuInferencePagedAttentionConfig()`, `ReferencePagedAttentionConfig()`) and parameterize on those directly instead of the string enum.

5. Estimated diff: ~400-600 lines across `tpu_kernels.py` (split into `paged_attention_config.py` + `tpu_pallas_backend.py`), `tpu_inference_adapter.py` (no signature change), `attention.py`, `llama.py`, `apertus.py`, two test files. Above the <100 LOC PR threshold, hence this design comment instead of a direct PR.

**Open questions for the issue author**

- Should the choice family base live in `levanter.inference` (next to backends) or in `levanter.layers.attention` (next to the call sites)?
- Is `AutoPagedAttentionConfig(candidates=[...])` the preferred way to express the current `AUTO` policy, or do you want a top-level `auto` choice that internally re-resolves to a platform-derived default each call?
- Confirm the `fail_on_reference_fallback` semantics belong on the base config rather than only on `ReferencePagedAttentionConfig` — keeping it on the base preserves today's "I picked tpu-inference and refuse to silently fall back to reference" behaviour.

Will wait for confirmation on #6099 merging and the questions above before opening a PR.

🤖
## Description
Add target-only PPL eval slices for low-level text and interpreter mechanics. The eval should cover exact token-to-character decomposition across every Marin tokenizer id that is representable in normal UTF-8 text, report byte-fallback/replacement-character ids that cannot round-trip through JSONL text, and include small circuit-style probes for character counts, indices, line lengths, indentation, arithmetic, and Python REPL surfaces.

### Definition of Done
- Generate eval-only JSONL records with `input`, `target`, and provenance metadata.
- Verify every representable non-special Marin tokenizer id included in vocab coverage appears in at least one rendered input as that token id.
- Emit a coverage summary for excluded ids that cannot be exposed as normal Unicode text.
- Register the bundle in the perplexity-gap registry for Marin 32B vs Qwen3 32B scoring.
- Add focused tests for tokenizer coverage verification, target-only rendering, metadata/tags, and local JSONL staging.
- Provide the dry-run/run command for the scoring job and record the output artifact paths when run.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue and check actionability
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (open PRs/issues)
- [x] Survey existing eval-slice pattern and registry
- [x] Post Research + Proposed Approach for human review
- [ ] Await design confirmation before implementation (scope exceeds the 100-line PR threshold for agent-authored fixes)

# Research

Issue asks for a new target-only PPL bundle covering tokenizer/interpreter mechanics (char counts, indices, line lengths, indentation, arithmetic, Python REPL) plus a vocab-coverage invariant over the Marin tokenizer, and registration in the perplexity-gap registry against the existing \`marin_32b\` vs \`qwen3_32b\` pair. No existing slice covers this — the closest analogs are the identifier-encoding and delimiter-format families.

Definition of done is concrete, but two design choices need a human decision before code lands: (a) storage surface for the bundle, and (b) what \"every non-special token id appears\" means in practice given the ~100k Marin vocab.

**Relevant code**
- [\`experiments/evals/synthetic_identifier_encoding_ppl.py\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/synthetic_identifier_encoding_ppl.py) — template for slice family + JSONL writer + sample harness
- [\`experiments/evals/synthetic_delimiter_format_ppl.py#L385-L411\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/synthetic_delimiter_format_ppl.py#L385-L411) — alternative pattern using local \`StepSpec\` materialization (no HF push)
- [\`experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py#L113-L183\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py#L113-L183) — bundle factories, \`registered_perplexity_gap_bundles\`, and the \`marin_32b\` / \`qwen3_32b\` pair already exist
- [\`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py#L116-L142\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py#L116-L142) — \`supervised_text_dataset\` is the target-only entry point
- [\`experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_coverage_matrix.py\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_coverage_matrix.py) — dry-run / run command; new bundle is picked up automatically once registered

# Proposed Approach

New module \`experiments/evals/circuit_coverage_ppl.py\` modeled on \`synthetic_identifier_encoding_ppl.py\`:

1. \`CircuitCoverageFamily(StrEnum)\` with six task families: \`vocab_coverage\`, \`char_counts\`, \`char_indices\`, \`line_lengths\`, \`indentation\`, \`arithmetic\`, \`python_repl\`. One \`CircuitCoveragePplSlice\` per family with tags \`loss:target_only\`, \`epic:5005\`, \`issue:6103\`, \`source:generated_circuit_coverage_ppl_v1\`, seed/examples, family/task.
2. Deterministic row generator (RNG seeded per row, same \`seed + slice_offset + row_index\` pattern) producing \`{input, target, id, subset, task, seed, metadata}\` JSONL records. Each family is small and probe-style:
   - \`char_counts\`: \"How many 'x' in 'abxxcx'? Answer: \" → \`3\\n\`
   - \`char_indices\`: \"The 4th char of 'abcdef' is \" → \`d\\n\`
   - \`line_lengths\`: \"Line length of 'foo bar baz': \" → \`11\\n\`
   - \`indentation\`: snippets with 2/4/8-space and tab leading prefixes; predict the continuation indent
   - \`arithmetic\`: small base-10 add/sub/mul, target is digits-only continuation
   - \`python_repl\`: short \`>>> expr\\n\` interactions where target is the next \`>>> \` line or the result
   - \`vocab_coverage\`: see below
3. **Vocab-coverage invariant**: load \`marin-community/marin-tokenizer\` once, enumerate \`{id: token}\` excluding \`all_special_ids\` and any \`added_tokens_decoder\` entries marked special. For each non-special id, emit a row whose rendered \`input + target\` re-tokenizes to a sequence containing that id at least once. Cheapest construction: \`tokenizer.decode([id])\` round-tripped through a fixed framing prompt (e.g. \`\"Token: \" + decoded + \"\\n\"\`), then verified by re-encoding under \`add_special_tokens=False\`. Rows where the round-trip drops the id (mojibake / merge boundary issues) get a fallback construction that places the decoded fragment between two known-stable anchor strings until the id reappears; if no construction works after N attempts, raise (fail fast — invariant must be true by construction, not by chance).
4. Tests in new \`tests/evals/test_circuit_coverage_ppl.py\`:
   - Tokenizer coverage: load tokenizer, generate \`vocab_coverage\` slice, assert \`{id} ⊆ tokens(input+target for every row)\` covers \`vocab − special_ids\`. Real tokenizer, no mocks.
   - Target-only rendering: every row has non-empty \`input\` and \`target\`; both keys round-trip through \`supervised_text_dataset\` and produce a \`RawTextEvaluationDataset\` with \`input_key=\"input\"\`, \`target_key=\"target\"\`.
   - Metadata/tags: each slice's \`tags\` tuple contains the required tags; \`metadata\` carries \`family\` and probe-specific keys.
   - Local JSONL staging: \`write_circuit_coverage_jsonl_configs(tmp_path)\` produces one file per slice, each line valid JSON with the required schema.
5. Registry: add \`circuit_coverage_bundle()\` in \`experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py\` and append it to \`registered_perplexity_gap_bundles()\`. The existing \`PerplexityGapPair(\"marin_32b\", \"qwen3_32b\")\` then picks it up automatically.
6. Scoring command (no new entry point needed):
   \`uv run python experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_coverage_matrix.py --dry_run\` for dry-run, drop \`--dry_run\` for the real run. Artifact paths land under \`analysis/model_perplexity_scores/circuit_coverage/{marin_32b,qwen3_32b}\` and \`analysis/perplexity_gap/circuit_coverage/marin_32b-vs-qwen3_32b\`.

# Open questions for the issue author

1. **Storage surface**: HF-hosted (like \`marin-community/synth-identifier-encoding-ppl\`) or local-only via \`StepSpec\` materialization (like \`synthetic_delimiter_format_ppl\`)? The latter avoids a new HF dataset repo and revision pin.
2. **Vocab-coverage size**: Marin tokenizer is ~100k tokens. One row per non-special id ≈ 100k rows for that slice alone. OK as the spec reads, but should we cap at a stratified sample (e.g. all unique tokens by frequency decile) to keep the bundle within \`max_docs_per_dataset=256\`? If kept at full coverage, the bundle needs a per-slice \`max_docs_per_dataset\` override.
3. **Python REPL surface**: scope to single-line \`>>> expr\` continuations, or include multi-line tracebacks / \`...\` continuations?

Implementation is straightforward and well-scoped once (1)-(3) are decided. Happy to proceed once confirmed.

🤖

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

B200 segmented FA4/CuTe attention now has a measured 8192-token BF16 kernel baseline for `B=1, S=8192, Hq=32, Hkv=8, D=128, segment_len=256`. The useful change is the SM100/B200 tile choice: keep `forward_tile=(128,64)` and use `backward_tile=(64,64)`. That patched FA4 path measured `1.021 ms` forward+backward, improving the original FA4 baseline (`1.666 ms`) by about 1.63x and beating the valid Transformer Engine `flash` comparison (`1.229 ms`) for forward+backward. Forward-only remains slightly slower than TE flash (`0.347 ms` FA4 versus `0.317 ms` TE flash). Treat TE `auto`/`fused` as blocked rather than as comparison data because both failed with mixed CUDA runtime libraries. Next step is to rerun timing across a small nearby B200 shape grid before considering the tile choice stable.

### Helpful links
- Current implementation PR: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5880
- Experiment branch: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/codex/fa4-cute-b200-research
- Parent GPU profile epic: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5608
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Scope

Track the B200 FA4/CuTe segmented attention kernel work for Grug dynamic packed segment IDs, with 8192 sequence length as the primary target. This issue follows the kernel-research workflow: correctness and gradient parity, compile-including timing, steady-state timing, bounded tile sweeps, and explicit comparison against the fastest available external baseline.

## Related GPU Perf Work

* Parent GPU profile epic: #5608
* Flash-like Grug attention target: #5610
* Dense-mask-free attention backward: #5658
* Reproducible B200 Grug-vs-Megatron profile: #5815
* B200 MoE GMM tuning: #5894
* Megatron throughput target and MFU follow-ups: #4311, #4302, #4312
* Current implementation PR: #5880

## Current Baseline

| Path | Forward | Forward+backward | Numerics vs reference | Notes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| FA4/CuTe baseline `(128,64)/(128,64)` | `0.350 ms` | `1.666 ms` | value `0.015625`, grad `0.0625` | Original SM100 tile choice |
| FA4/CuTe patched `(128,64)/(64,64)` | `0.347 ms` | `1.021 ms` | value `0.015625`, grad `0.0625` | Current PR #5880 path |
| TE flash THD packed sequence | `0.317 ms` | `1.229 ms` | value `0.015625`, grad `0.0625` | Valid external comparison; TE fused/auto blocked |

Confidence: replicated for this one B200 target shape; not yet stable across a wider shape grid.

## Decision Log

* 2026-05-20: use B200/SM100 `forward_tile=(128,64)`; `forward_tile=(128,128)` was much slower on the segmented BSHD/GQA target shape.
* 2026-05-20: use B200/SM100 `backward_tile=(64,64)`; focused sweep and direct patched benchmark both showed about `1.63x` faster forward+backward than `(128,64)` backward with unchanged small-reference numerics.
* 2026-05-20: treat TE `flash` as the current external comparison. TE `auto` and `fused` remain blocked by a CUDA runtime library conflict and should not be used for gap claims yet.
* 2026-05-21: PR #5880 is green with the attention-relevant implementation and focused tests.

## Negative Results Index

* Wider forward tile `(128,128)` regressed the 8192 segmented B200 shape badly: forward about `4.386 ms`, forward+backward about `5.686 ms`.
* One B200 benchmark attempt failed during JAX CUDA device initialization with `CUDA_ERROR_UNKNOWN`; the same patch passed focused correctness and later benchmarked on another B200.
* TE `auto` and `fused` failed with `Multiple libcudart libraries found: libcudart.so.12 and libcudart.so.13`, including in a cleaner TE-only environment.

## Next Steps

* Re-run B200 timing on a small shape grid around the 8192 target before calling the tile choice stable.
* If TE fused becomes important, diagnose the CUDA runtime conflict in a clean environment and repeat the comparison.
* Keep issue updates append-only with exact command, hardware (`B200`), dtype, shape, compile time, steady-state time, and max/mean numeric deltas.
* If this evolves into a broader tuned-table kernel, add stable bucket definitions and an explicit fallback/autotune-on-miss plan per the kernel workflow.

## Research Logbook Snapshot

Local logbook path: `.agents/logbooks/fa4-cute-b200.md`. Snapshot below preserves the experiment notes that produced the current numbers.

<details>
<summary>fa4-cute-b200.md</summary>

issues.body:
**TL;DR.** We ran the Snowball E11 RL regimen against `Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507` to check whether the SkyRL/Iris training path holds at 235B on a third-party MoE. It does: six full optimizer steps on 96 H100s with no OOM, no rank drop, no NCCL abort, and importance-sampling ratios that stayed at 1.000. The run produced no learning signal, and we stopped it at step 6 of 50. The cause was a generation budget sized for a different model — 55% of samples hit the 8,192-token cap instead of finishing — so the objective was dominated by a truncation penalty rather than by correctness. Steps took ~9 hours each, 3× our pre-registered throughput limit.

## Setup

Port of the E11 regimen (DeepScaleR, 39,304 rows; `aime` verifier; batch 256 × 16 samples; 10,240-token window = 2,048 input + 8,192 generation; DAPO clip 0.2/0.4 with the dynamic-sampling filter; TIS cap 2.0) from Marin's 67B-A2B Grug to `Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507` @ `6cbffae6`. Run `rl-qwen3-235b-a22b-thinking-2507-rno2a-d-20260822-140923-13aad3`, launched 2026-08-22 14:09 UTC.

Geometry: 12 × H100x8 = 96 GPUs — 8 policy nodes (FSDP2, EP 1, `cpu_offload` on) and 4 inference engines at TP 8. Weights staged from an in-region S3 mirror, 118 safetensors, 438 GB.

## What held up

The stack ran a 235B third-party MoE end to end. Each risk we wrote down before launching came back clean on the systems side:

- No OOM at init or in any backward pass, on 64 GPUs with `cpu_offload`.
- No runaway dynamic-sampling discard; generation completed every step and never hit the `max_sample_batches` stop.
- TIS agreed closely between trainer and vLLM: `imp_ratio_mean` 1.000, `|log r|` 0.043, token `|Δlog p|` μ/p99 0.0139 / 0.128.
- Checkpoint volume stayed inside its budget at 4.8 TiB across 601 objects on a TTL prefix.

We had not previously trained a model this size, or a non-Marin MoE, on this path. That part of the question is answered.

## Timings

From the driver log, per-step wall-clock:

| step | logged (UTC) | Δ |
| ---: | --- | ---: |
| 1 | 08-23 00:30:59 | 10 h 22 m from submit (incl. bring-up and the streamed 438 GB EP load) |
| 2 | 08-23 09:32:34 | 9 h 02 m |
| 3 | 08-23 18:24:53 | 8 h 52 m |
| 4 | 08-24 03:32:10 | 9 h 07 m |
| 5 | 08-24 12:41:44 | 9 h 09 m |
| 6 | 08-24 21:40:08 | 8 h 58 m |

~9 hours per step, σ ≈ 7 minutes across the five intervals. Bring-up to first step-1 metrics was 10 h 22 m, of which about 1 h 20 m is scheduling plus the expert-parallel load and the rest is the step itself.

Six steps cost 59.6 hours on 96 GPUs, roughly 5,700 GPU-hours. The 50-step horizon would have run ~19 days holding 19% of the cluster. We had set `> 3 h/step` as the line where throughput becomes the problem.

## Why there was no learning signal

| step | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `environment/acc` | 0.3218 | 0.3381 | 0.2805 | 0.3193 | 0.2805 | 0.3167 |
| `reward/avg_raw_reward` | −0.049 | −0.145 | −0.011 | −0.039 | −0.138 | −0.084 |
| `policy/policy_entropy` | 0.1080 | 0.1066 | 0.1061 | 0.1061 | 0.1072 | 0.1071 |

Accuracy oscillates in a 0.28–0.34 band with no direction, reward is flat to slightly negative, and entropy is flat to three decimals. `avg_pass_at_16` reads 1.0000 at every step, but that is measured after the dynamic-sampling filter has dropped uninformative groups, so it carries no signal here.

At step 6, `stop_reason/length` was 2,241 against `stop_reason/stop` 1,855 out of 4,096 samples: 54.7% of generations never terminated, with mean response length 6,282 tokens against the 8,192 cap. Non-termination rose from 0.491 at the first read to 0.547; we had set 0.3 as the gate.

That is the whole result. More than half of every batch was scored on a truncation penalty instead of on whether the answer was right, so the gradient was mostly about length. It also explains the step time: over half the samples ran to the cap, paying full generation cost and returning nothing usable.

The mismatch is structural. `Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507` emits long chain-of-thought by design, and we gave it a window sized for a 67B-A2B model. Both available fixes cost more than this arm was worth: a larger generation budget makes a 9-hour step longer, and turning thinking off trains something other than the model we wanted to evaluate.

## Where we landed

Stopped at step 6 by owner decision. No checkpoint was exported and no held-out evaluation was run, so there is no model artifact or downstream score to report. Logs, traces, trajectories, and the resolved config are preserved; the run's S3 prefixes have been deleted.

If we come back to this: size the window to the model instead of inheriting it from the previous experiment. A thinking variant needs a budget above its natural trace length — 16k or more, given a 6.3k mean while truncated — which at this geometry means accepting a step time well past 9 hours, or a smaller model, or more inference engines. Both gates we set beforehand fired at step 1; we should have acted on them then rather than at step 6.

issues.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

comments.body:
🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

| rung | racks | batch | steps | tokens | active |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d768 | 1 | 1024 | 11,420 | 48B | 61M |
| d1024 | 2 | 2048 | 15,276 | 128B | 162M |
| d1536 | 6 | 6144 | 15,128 | 381B | 481M |
| d2048 | 11 | 11,264 | 20,072 | 926B | 1.2B |
| **d6144 (hero)** | 11 | 11,264 | 390,139 | **18.0T** | 22.8B |

## 6. Code (at run commit [`12d8b6f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be))

**Model** ([`model.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py)) — [`GrugModelConfig`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L160)
- All-MoE routed FFN: [`MoEMLP`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L907) · shared experts [`DenseMLP`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L637)
- QB routing (histogram estimator): threshold/beta [`_qb_beta_hist`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L874), histogram build [`_histogram_from_expert_counts`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L820), applied next-step as stop-grad bias
- Sigmoid combine + renorm-to-2.5: [`_ROUTING_RENORM_SUM`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L58), [combine](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L980)
- LatentMoE + learnable latent RMSNorm: [`latent_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1046)
- RMSNorm on embeddings/readout: [`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223), [`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1203); [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594)
- GatedNorm: [`GatedNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L612)
- XSA (exclusive self-attention): [subtract V-parallel component](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L573)

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

comments.body: Comparing our scaling law to prior runs. The main differences here is that the May recipe is at compute optimal, this run is at ~12x overtrained, and the 67B-A2B scaling law was at 100x overtrained. The 67B-A2B ran at 8k seqlen, and was therefore given a lower asympotote of 1.4 instead of 1.5. The May fit also inaccurately has an asympotote at 1.6 instead of 1.5. Main architecture change is we dropped from 4/256 level of sparsity to 4/192 level of sparsity (25% fewer total parameters, to fit on GB200 at this scale. Several other small features added. Overall, the scaling law looks reasonable and nothing looks off in the training dynamics or data. Grad norms look stable over the run, peaking at 25% into the run. These runs ran at oversized batch sizes, which may be slightly suppressing the gradient. Expecting the grad norm to climb higher on the hero run, but still peak at the same ~25% into the run. This will be good metric to monitor for issues. Drop rate jumps to 10 pct at very start, then drops to 0, then climbs to ~4pct over the run. Slightly increasing as we scale. Predicting we wont have that 10 percent spike for the hero, because our warmup (1 percent) will cover a much larger number of steps since the hero is at a higher step count. I think most likely scenario is the hero runs around 2 percent dropping, but up to 8 percent seems plausible bsaed on the data at 4k seqlen.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

issues.body:
As of #7820 the expert FF parameters are stored in a big `[n_layers, n_experts, d_in, d_out]` tensor, eg `[48, 384, 3072, 3072]`, with the specialised [`_newtonschulz_4d_distributed`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5da0277745729230801f91e0181406f291099f9d/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/grugmuon_hero.py#L211) computing Newton Schulz on the last two dimensions.

However, in the optimizer, the axes used to compute the norm will end up as `(1,2,3)`, which includes the expert dimension.

https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5da0277745729230801f91e0181406f291099f9d/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py#L76

This seems to be unintentional, since that optimizer code was originally to handle 3D `[n_experts, d_in, d_out]` shapes in #6153.

The implication is that an updated matrix parameter **M**<sub>t+1</sub> will **no longer be constrained to its original hypersphere** of norm ||**M**<sub>t</sub>||<sub>F</sub> as described in MuonH originally. Instead the combined cat([**M**<sub>t+1</sub><sup>expert1</sup>, **M**<sub>t+1</sub><sup>expert2</sup>, ...]) will be constrained to norm ||cat([**M**<sub>t</sub><sup>expert1</sup>, **M**<sub>t</sub><sup>expert2</sup>, ...])||<sub>F</sub> allowing individual matrices to grow or shrink within that constraint. Although not necessarily a terrible thing to do (experiments in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5253 tried both for AdamH).

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
The expert-parallel ring MoE backend (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py`, `_moe_mlp_ep_ring_local`) computes wrong outputs. Against an exact fp32 dense MoE reference on a GB200 node with mesh `(data=2, expert=2, model=1)`, E=8 experts (4 per shard), top-2, 64 tokens/device, H=64, I=96, bf16, capacity factor 2.0 (both implementations report zero drops), ring's forward deviates by 0.75x-0.93x relative on most seeds and produced values of magnitude 2.3e28 on one seed; its gradients contain NaN. The ragged all-to-all backend on identical inputs matches the dense reference to 0.4-0.5% (bf16 noise) with clean gradients, so the harness and inputs are not the cause. This matters because ring is the implementation other backends are validated against (`test_moe_mlp_ragged_matches_ring_with_ep_axis_when_available` skips on CPU, so the EP path is effectively untested in CI).

A second defect: at capacity factor 4.0 in the same configuration, `jax.lax.top_k(selection_key, local_capacity)` at `ep_ring.py:88` requests k=512 from a 256-row selection pool and crashes; `local_capacity` is not capped at the gathered pool size.

Reproduce:
1. On branch `research/mcwitt/8317-ragged-tune`, submit `python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.ragged_ep_check --version dev --run` (needs 4 GB200s; the check compares ring, ragged, and the exact dense reference).
2. Read `ring_vs_dense` in the `ragged_ep_seed` log lines.

Expected: ring matches the dense fp32 reference within bf16 tolerance at a capacity factor where nothing drops, at any mesh shape.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

I reproduced both defects on current `main` with four GB200s. At capacity 2.0, ring had 0 drops but forward relative max error was 0.79, 0.90, 0.96, and 1.93 across seeds 0–3; seed 1 produced non-finite gradients. Forcing `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=xla` reduced those errors to 0.005–0.007 with finite gradients, isolating the corruption to the Triton ragged-dot kernel: its physical power-of-two tiles read and write past logical M/N/K boundaries. Capacity 4.0 separately requests `top_k(k=512)` from 256 rows.

**Relevant code**
- [`ragged_dot.py#L103-L135`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L103-L135) - unmasked forward tiles
- [`ragged_dot.py#L179-L210`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L179-L210) - unmasked weight-gradient tiles
- [`ep_ring.py#L56-L88`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py#L56-L88) - uncapped selection capacity
- [`test_grugformer_moe.py#L957-L1012`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/tests/grug/test_grugformer_moe.py#L957-L1012) - ring used as oracle

# Proposed Fix

Mask edge reads and writes in both Triton ragged-dot layouts, and cap ring's selection capacity at the gathered assignment pool size. Replace ring-as-oracle coverage with value and gradient comparisons against a direct dense `einsum` MoE reference; retain backend-to-backend checks only as secondary diagnostics. Exercise ring at excess capacity to cover the crash, and validate the portable ring, ragged all-to-all, fixed all-to-all, and pooled-wave paths against the dense reference where their runtimes are available.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body: 🤖 Draft fix: #8610. Masking logical Triton tile boundaries reduced ring's four-seed GB200 forward error from 0.79–1.93 to 0.005–0.007, restored finite gradients within 0.006 of the fp32 dense reference, and made capacity factor 4.0 succeed. EP tests now use a direct dense MoE oracle; ring, fixed all-to-all, and pooled-wave have cross-shard value/gradient coverage, while ragged runs the same check on supported accelerator runtimes. Current `main` still segfaults inside XLA's ragged all-to-all on stock GB200 before parity can be measured, and DeepEP's external FFI transport remains outside portable end-to-end tests.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Build RiffleEval as a paired long-context evaluation of coherent stream tracking. Each base item keeps the source text, question, answer, distractors, and token budget fixed while changing document chunks from blocked to riffled order. The primary result is the per-item riffle penalty, sliced by foreign-chunk interference count and token distance.

UncheatableEval is a candidate source feed after revision pinning, token-length filtering, license review, and safety filtering. Its current Marin integration is unsuitable: it downloads a stale GitHub fork whose records are capped at 5,000 characters and supplies no questions or evidence annotations. For v0, use frozen natural documents with exact-answer factual overlays; evaluate a filtered UncheatableEval `-Long` subset as one source arm, beginning with English Wikipedia and permissively licensed documents.

## Description

Long-context evaluations such as NIAH often test retrieval of one conspicuous item from a large context. RiffleEval tests whether a model can maintain several ordered information streams whose chunks repeatedly alternate across a 32K–64K prompt, then reconstruct facts within one stream.

For source document \(D_i = [C_{i,1}, \ldots, C_{i,n}]\), generate a legal merge that preserves chunk order within each source. Every chunk receives an opaque, per-example stream ID and ordinal. Questions and evidence annotations are created and verified against the clean document before riffling.

Each base item produces these conditions:

1. Clean target document, for source-task competence.
2. Blocked full context, with the target and distractor documents contiguous.
3. Riffled full context, with identical content and prompt budget.
4. Adjacent-evidence control for multi-evidence items.

The v0 task families are single-stream exact QA and two-evidence within-stream integration. Cross-stream joins and continuation NLL remain follow-ups.

The proposed context-length and stream-count matrix is not a full Cartesian product. With 4K–8K source documents, 32K supports roughly 4–8 streams and 64K supports roughly 8–16 streams. Larger documents or additional filler semantics would be required to hold stream count fixed while scaling total context. The generator must reject infeasible cells instead of silently repeating or padding sources.

## Hypothesis or Goal

At fixed content and question difficulty, riffling causes a measurable accuracy loss beyond the loss caused by the same blocked distractors. The loss increases with the number of intervening foreign chunks after controlling for absolute token distance. Better long-context checkpoints should move the retention curve toward larger interference counts.

## Status

Background research is complete. No implementation or model run has started.

### Proposed v0

- 250–500 verified base items, expanded into deterministic paired variants.
- 32K and 64K contexts; feasible 4/8/16-stream cells; approximately 512-token chunks.
- Exact short answers with one-evidence and two-evidence overlays.
- Opaque opening and closing markers with tokenizer-balanced random IDs.
- Random and same-domain distractors.
- Native-model score with tools disabled.
- Exact match, per-item riffle penalty, blocked-to-riffled penalty, and retention curves by token distance, interference count, evidence count, and active streams.
- Target-stream extraction and oracle-evidence diagnostics to separate stream selection from reasoning.
- Frozen generator version, seed, source revision/hash, tokenizer, prompt, and structural metadata for every item.

### UncheatableEval corpus decision

Use it as an optional source-discovery and freshness feed. Do not use the published collection as the sole corpus or reuse `experiments/datasets/uncheatable.py`.

The current upstream `-Long` snapshots contain 7,500 records across 15 categories and retain source URL, date, category, `content`, and `untruncated_content`. They provide recent natural interference, but no question, answer, stable ID, evidence span, or hop graph. The dataset card declares no dataset license, and source rights differ by document. AO3 has safety concerns; arbitrary GitHub files need license and secret checks; BBC is a poor redistribution default; PDF extraction can corrupt arXiv text. Freshness only protects models whose training cutoff predates the crawl.

A derived arm must:

- pin the Hugging Face revision and content hash;
- filter on benchmark-tokenizer length, language, quality, and safety;
- record URL, collection date, source category, license, and transformed-text hash;
- begin with English Wikipedia and individually cleared permissive sources;
- exclude BBC and AO3 from v0;
- generate exact-answer overlays and frozen evidence spans against the exact transformed text.

## Background Research Brief

- Effort / stop rule / date: medium; 2026-08-24; stopped when the internal, benchmark, corpus, and contradiction passes no longer changed the v0 recommendation.

### Current Marin context

- #7638 owns RULER integration. RiffleEval should not duplicate its eval harness work.
- #4736 specified the closest reusable data contract: frozen long-document QA items with exact answers, evidence spans, and length bins.
- #7181 found that retained MRCR context reduced final-turn PPL from 21.0855 to 10.4012 at 8,192 tokens. Its extraction PR #7203 closed unmerged, so it is prior evidence rather than current infrastructure.
- #5825 previously built 32K/64K long-document PPL slices; the implementation was later removed by #6633.
- No existing issue or implementation tests repeated switching among several coherent streams.

### External prior art

- [RULER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654) varies context length and task complexity across multi-needle retrieval, variable tracking, aggregation, and QA. RiffleEval adds coherent natural streams and a paired blocked/riffled intervention.
- [MRCR/Michelangelo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640) shows that repeated, similar requests and ordinal selection are harder than unique needles. RiffleEval should include similar competing streams and report random/noise floors.
- [NoLiMa](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05167) shows that lexical overlap makes retrieval easier and normalizes long-context scores to short-context competence. RiffleEval should vary lexical overlap and reject items with weak clean-document accuracy.
- [BABILong](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/c0d62e70dbc659cc9bd44cbcf1cb652f-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf) distributes multi-fact synthetic tasks through natural books. RiffleEval adds several foreground streams, explicit stream identities, and the same task before and after structural transformation.
- [LOFT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13121) found that marker and prompt formatting materially affect retrieval. Marker tokenization and query placement must be fixed or explicitly ablated.
- [UncheatableEval](https://github.com/Jellyfish042/uncheatable_eval) evaluates rolling internet text by NLL. Its freshness method is useful for source discovery; it does not provide RiffleEval annotations.

### Contradiction and shortcut pass

- Random riffles and IDs prevent fixed-order contamination but do not prevent a model from answering public facts from parametric memory. Synthetic counterfactual overlays provide the durable control.
- Opaque IDs expose segmentation but do not prevent keyword search within the target stream. Lexical-overlap and near-neighbor distractor slices remain necessary.
- “Uniform-ish” legal merges do not independently control gap length. Sample examples from explicit interference-count and token-distance strata.
- Marker token lengths can differ across tokenizers and become an unplanned treatment. Balance marker encodings and store their token counts.
- Native QA generation from unannotated documents can admit one-passage shortcuts. Require evidence spans, clean-document verification, and minimal-evidence ablations.

### Recommended next experiments

#### 1. Validate the paired structural signal at 32K

- Minimum experiment / baseline: 100 overlay items, four streams, 512-token chunks; clean, blocked, and riffled conditions on two representative models with different long-context capability.
- Expected signal / falsifier: a nonzero blocked-to-riffled penalty that grows across interference buckets while clean accuracy remains high. Near-zero penalty, floor-level clean accuracy, or prompt-format sensitivity larger than the treatment falsifies the current setup.

#### 2. Add two-evidence integration and 64K

- Minimum experiment / baseline: two controlled facts in widely separated chunks; adjacent-evidence and oracle-extracted-stream baselines; feasible 8/16-stream cells.
- Expected signal / falsifier: two-evidence retention degrades faster than one-evidence retention while oracle extraction recovers most accuracy. Failure of the oracle indicates base reasoning or question-construction problems.

#### 3. Compare source pools

- Minimum experiment / baseline: matched overlays over a pinned filtered UncheatableEval `-Long` arm and one stable, license-cleared long-document corpus.
- Expected signal / falsifier: model ranking and riffle penalty remain stable across source pools. Large domain-specific reversals require a multi-corpus benchmark or removal of the unstable source.

### Source ledger

| Source | Type | Location | Claim used for | Confidence | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RULER | paper | https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654 | complexity axes and baselines | high | nearest variable-tracking precedent |
| Michelangelo / MRCR | paper and official code | https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640 | repeated similar needles and order | high | conversation format differs from riffled documents |
| NoLiMa | paper | https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05167 | lexical-overlap shortcut and retention normalization | high | single-association retrieval |
| BABILong | paper | https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/c0d62e70dbc659cc9bd44cbcf1cb652f-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf | distributed multi-fact reasoning in natural text | high | one background stream |
| LOFT | paper | https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13121 | formatting and identifier sensitivity | high | fixed retrieval corpora |
| UncheatableEval | official repo and dataset | https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jellyfish042/UncheatableEval-2026-07-Long | source schema, freshness, and corpus limitations | high | no dataset-level license or QA annotations |
| Marin #4736 | GitHub issue | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4736 | QA manifest and evidence schema | high | closed before implementation |
| Marin #7638 | GitHub issue | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7638 | active RULER scope | high | avoid duplicate harness work |
| Marin #7181 | GitHub issue | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7181 | paired MRCR PPL result | high | extraction PR closed unmerged |

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates: #7638, #4736, #7181, #5825

## Decision Log

- 2026-08-24: scope v0 to paired single-stream exact QA and two-evidence within-stream integration at 32K/64K.
- 2026-08-24: treat UncheatableEval as an optional filtered source arm; reject the current Marin handle and the unfiltered published corpus as the canonical benchmark source.
- 2026-08-24: defer cross-stream joins, continuation NLL, and 128K+ until the primary structural signal is validated.

## Conclusion

Open. Advance to implementation if the 32K pilot produces high clean accuracy, a reproducible blocked-to-riffled penalty, and a stable ordering across source pools and marker templates.

spillover_issues.author: claude[bot]
spillover_issues.body:
The scheduled TPU canary ferry failed at the **Submit canary ferry** step; every later step was skipped. The iris job-run command produced no job id, so no training run started and no W&B run was created.

The controller rejected the launcher's LaunchJob immediately as unschedulable. The launcher carries two mutually exclusive constraints:

- **availability:v5p-8 exists** — from the launcher submit's reserve flag, which reserves the primary requested TPU variant (v5p-8).
- **preemptible==false** — auto-applied by the executor heuristic, because the launcher is a small CPU-only job (--cpu=1 --memory=2G, 1 replica, no accelerator) that matches looks_like_executor (lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py:905, thresholds <=1 core / <=4 GiB / <=1 replica).

v5p pools are preemptible-only, so the only two groups offering availability:v5p-8 (tpu_v5p-preemptible_8-us-central1-a, tpu_v5p-preemptible_8-us-east5-a) fail preemptible==false, while every non-preemptible group fails availability:v5p-8. No single scaling group satisfies both, so the job is rejected at submit rather than left pending. The controller was healthy: many other jobs submitted successfully in the same window.

**Regression:** #8605 (merged 2026-08-23, two days before this run) introduced the launcher reservation — "The TPU ferry now uses the primary requested TPU variant as an empirical availability reservation for its CPU launcher." Because the primary variant v5p-8 is preemptible-only and the launcher is auto-pinned non-preemptible, the reservation can never be satisfied.

Reproduce:
1. On main at/after #8605, run the Marin - Canary Ferry workflow (or its submit step): iris job run --no-wait --cpu=1 --memory=2G --disk=4G --priority production --reserve v5p-8 -- python -m experiments.ferries.canary_ferry
2. The controller rejects LaunchJob with "is unschedulable: no scaling group matches all constraints".
3. The submit step exits non-zero with no job id; the run fails.

Expected: the launcher schedules on a CPU pool and submits the training job.

<details>
<summary>Controller rejection (controller-iris-controller-marin.log, 06:43:56)</summary>

```
RPC LaunchJob failed after 841ms: Job /runner/iris-run-job-20260825-064353 is unschedulable: no scaling group matches all constraints.
constraint coverage across 82 group(s):
  preemptible==false: 19/82 satisfy
  availability:v5p-8 exists: 2/82 satisfy
closest group(s) each fail 1 of 2 constraint(s):
  fail [availability:v5p-8 exists]: cpu_vm_e2_highmem_2_ondemand-europe-west4-a, ... +14 more
  fail [preemptible==false]: tpu_v5p-preemptible_8-us-central1-a, tpu_v5p-preemptible_8-us-east5-a
    (constraints: preemptible EQ false, availability:v5p-8 EXISTS)
```
</details>

Possible fixes (not yet implemented): reserve a variant that has a non-preemptible pool (e.g. v4-8) instead of the preemptible-only primary; pass --preemptible on the launcher so the executor heuristic does not pin it; or propagate the launcher region without an availability reservation.

### Canary run context

- **Lane:** tpu
- **Iris job ID:** none — submission was rejected before a job was created (controller-assigned name /runner/iris-run-job-20260825-064353)
- **GHA run:** https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/32818177770
- **W&B run:** none created; intended RUN_ID was canary-tpu-32818177770-1
- **Date:** 2026-08-25

spillover_issues.body:
🤖 *(filed by an agent on behalf of @penfever)*

## Motivation

[#6136](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6136) demonstrated that `tpu-inference`'s vllm-impl (torch-XLA) path produces catastrophic decode (72-93% trace failures) on multi-host `v5p-32` + DP=2 + `max_num_seqs ≥ 4` for Qwen3.5-122B-FP8. The same hardware/orchestration stack serves Gemma4-31B cleanly because Gemma takes the **`flax_nnx`** path — a fully native JAX/Flax implementation that bypasses torch-XLA compilation entirely.

Until the upstream bug is fixed, the only safe way to serve a newly-released HF model at the scales we care about is to **port it to Haliax/Equinox** (Levanter's flax-native model framework) and serve it through `tpu-inference`'s `flax_nnx` path. We already have the underlying recipe ([`port-models.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/docs/recipes/port-models.md) + the long-form [`Port-Models.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/docs/dev/Port-Models.md)) but no playbook framed for the agent-as-author case, and no explicit linkage to the "do this to avoid the buggy torch-XLA serving path" framing.

## Deliverable

A new agent skill at `.agents/skills/port-model-to-flax/SKILL.md` following the existing skill format (see `.agents/skills/add-pallas-kernel/SKILL.md` for shape — frontmatter `name:` + `description:`, narrative body, references to canonical docs).

The skill should walk an agent through:

1. **Triage** — when is porting worth it? Decision flowchart: (a) HF model, (b) needs multi-host TPU serving OR `max_num_seqs ≥ 4`, (c) no existing flax_nnx implementation in `tpu-inference` → port. Otherwise skip.
2. **Reference reading** — point at `port-models.md` (concise) + `Port-Models.md` (long-form) + `llama.py` / `mixtral.py` as canonical examples.
3. **Implementation checklist** — config (`HFCompatConfig`), modules (`Embedding` / `Block` / `Transformer` / `LMHead` via `equinox.Module` + `haliax.NamedArray`), state-dict round-trip helpers (`_state_dict_key_map`, `to_state_dict` / `from_state_dict`), register with `LmConfig.register_subclass`.
4. **Numerics gates** — `chex.assert_trees_all_close` tolerances `1e-4` (complex modules) / `1e-5` (simple modules) per the recipe; never relax without explicit approval; per-module unit tests against the HF counterpart before full-stack comparison.
5. **Serving integration** — how to register the new flax model in `tpu-inference` so it picks the `flax_nnx` path; how to verify at runtime (`MODEL_IMPL_TYPE=auto` resolves to `flax_nnx`; log line on serve confirms).
6. **Validation harness** — round-trip serialization + output parity vs HF model on small inputs; once that passes, end-to-end trace-quality smoke (32k context, seqs=64, sample ~10 trajectories, manual / programmatic eyeball for incoherence/repetition along the same axes as the [Qwen audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6136)).

## Acceptance criteria

- `.agents/skills/port-model-to-flax/SKILL.md` exists and follows the peer skills' frontmatter shape (`name:` + `description:`).
- References the two existing port-models docs explicitly with file paths.
- Cross-links #6136 in the motivation so the next agent knows why this skill exists.
- Includes a `# Quickstart` block listing the minimal commands an agent runs end-to-end on a small test model (e.g. a tiny LLaMA-shaped release) for a smoke pass through all six steps above.
- Does NOT actually port a model — that's a separate issue once the skill lands.

## Out of scope

- Performing any specific port (Qwen 3.5, MiniMax, etc.) — those are individual follow-up issues that should *use* this skill.
- Fixing the upstream vllm-impl bug — tracked at #6136.
- Rewriting `port-models.md` itself unless gaps are discovered while writing the skill.

## Related

- #6136 — torch-XLA decode bug; motivation for this skill
- [`lib/levanter/docs/recipes/port-models.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/docs/recipes/port-models.md)
